interview.question: How do you enable multi-session support?
interview.answer: The server registers multiSession(), while the browser client registers multiSessionClient(). The client plugin enables management of multiple active sessions in the browser.
interview.followUp: What does the plugin use to preserve the additional sessions? It adds another browser cookie when a user logs in, and that cookie maintains the additional sessions.

interview.question: How do you switch between accounts?
interview.answer: Call listDeviceSessions to obtain the active sessions for the current user. Then pass a selected session's token to setActive to make it the active session.
interview.followUp: Which endpoint corresponds to listing sessions? The operation uses GET /multi-session/list-device-sessions.

interview.question: How is the session limit configured?
interview.answer: The plugin accepts maximumSessions to limit how many sessions a user can have. If omitted, the documented default is five sessions per device.
interview.followUp: What happens when the user signs out? The existing signOut method automatically revokes all active sessions for that user.

keyPoints: It supports simultaneous account sessions inside one browser, so users can change accounts without repeatedly authenticating.
It fits account-switching interfaces where remaining signed in to several accounts is part of the workflow.
Client-side management requires adding multiSessionClient() to the Better Auth client configuration.
A login causes the plugin to add an extra browser cookie used for the additional session state.
Use listDeviceSessions to retrieve the active sessions associated with the current device and user.
Use setActive with a session token when the user chooses which account should become active.
gotchas: Calling the existing sign-out flow removes every active session for that user, not only the currently active one.
The default device limit is five sessions; configure maximumSessions when a different cap is required.

nextCookies.summary: `nextCookies` is a Better Auth plugin for Next.js server actions. It automatically applies authentication cookies emitted through `Set-Cookie` response headers.
nextCookies.explanation: The `nextCookies` plugin integrates Better Auth with Next.js server actions. It watches authentication responses and uses Next.js cookie handling to apply any `Set-Cookie` headers automatically, allowing operations such as email sign-in or sign-up to establish cookies without manually calling the Next.js cookies helper.

example.title: Enable nextCookies in Next.js
example.explanation: Register the plugin last in the Better Auth plugin list so server actions can apply cookies emitted by authentication responses.

useCases.title: Server-action sign-in
useCases.scenario: A Next.js server action performs email authentication and must persist the resulting session cookie.

useCases.title: Server-action sign-up
useCases.scenario: A Next.js server action creates an account and needs the new authentication state stored in cookies.

useCases.title: Automatic response-cookie handling
useCases.scenario: An application wants response cookies from Better Auth API calls bridged into Next.js cookie handling without custom plumbing.

interview.question: What problem does nextCookies solve?
interview.answer: It is a Next.js integration plugin for Better Auth server actions. It automatically applies cookies whenever an authentication response includes a `Set-Cookie` header.
interview.followUp: Why is plugin order relevant? The documented configuration requires this plugin to be last, so later plugins do not interfere with its response-cookie handling.

interview.question: Why is this needed in a server action?
interview.answer: Next.js server actions do not automatically set cookies from Better Auth responses because cookie mutation must use Next.js's `cookies` helper. The plugin handles that integration automatically.
interview.followUp: Which operations benefit? Server-side operations that need to establish or update authentication cookies, such as email sign-in and sign-up.

interview.question: How do you configure it?
interview.answer: Import `nextCookies` from `better-auth/next-js`, call it in the `plugins` array, and put it at the end of that array. After that, cookie-setting authentication calls can update cookies automatically.
interview.followUp: What should remain separate? Middleware or proxy session checks should not be treated as full session validation; protected actions still require server-side validation.

keyPoints: Use the plugin when Better Auth calls run in Next.js server actions and need to persist authentication cookies.
Cookie synchronization is triggered by a `Set-Cookie` response header.
After installation, cookie-setting Better Auth functions update the Next.js cookie store without extra cookie code.
Typical affected calls include email sign-in and email sign-up invoked from server actions.
gotchas: Place `nextCookies()` last in the Better Auth plugin array; the documentation explicitly requires that ordering.

oAuthProxy.explanation: oAuthProxy adds a routing layer for OAuth sign-ins from trusted previews and local development. The participating environment sends the flow through the production callback server, which uses the registered production OAuth callback and returns the result to the originating deployment.

interview.question: What problem does oAuthProxy solve?
interview.answer: oAuthProxy lets one OAuth client serve local development and preview deployments whose callback URLs are variable. The production server receives the provider callback, exchanges the authorization code, and returns encrypted profile data to the originating deployment.
interview.followUp: How is the OAuth provider configured? Register only the production callback URL; the proxy routes preview and development requests through that callback.

interview.question: How should the plugin be configured across environments?
interview.answer: Configure the plugin with the production callback server URL and a dedicated secret. Use the same configuration and secret on production, previews, and localhost.
interview.followUp: Why must the secret match? The participating environments use it to communicate securely during the proxied flow.

interview.question: Which callback URL should be registered with the provider?
interview.answer: The OAuth provider needs only the callback URL on the production domain. Preview and development callbacks are routed through production automatically by the plugin.
interview.followUp: What deployment requirement follows? Only trusted environments should participate, and each must have the plugin installed and the shared secret configured.

keyPoints: Use the plugin when local or preview callback URLs are dynamic and cannot conveniently be registered with the provider.
A single OAuth client can support multiple non-production environments through the fixed production callback.
Production completes the provider exchange and sends the resulting profile data back to the requesting environment.
OAuth authorization requests from trusted non-production deployments are routed through production.
Provider configuration does not require separate callback registrations for every preview deployment.
After setup, routing from previews and local development to production is automatic.

Register the provider callback on the production domain rather than each preview or local URL.
The plugin must be installed wherever the proxy flow participates, not only on production.

interview.question: What does `oidcProvider` do?
interview.answer: `oidcProvider` turns a Better Auth server into an OpenID Connect provider. It is added to the `plugins` array and can receive options such as `loginPage`.
interview.followUp: How can clients be registered? Use `oauth2.register` on the client or `auth.api.registerOAuthApplication` on the server.

interview.question: How do clients obtain user information?
interview.answer: The plugin exposes a UserInfo endpoint at `/oauth2/userinfo`. Clients must send a valid access token to retrieve authenticated-user information.
interview.followUp: What prerequisite does the endpoint enforce? The access token must be valid and associated with the client’s authenticated flow.

interview.question: What setup step is required after adding the plugin?
interview.answer: After configuration, the database schema must be migrated or generated so Better Auth can create the required fields and tables. This is part of installation rather than an optional cleanup step.
interview.followUp: How can public clients register themselves? Set `allowDynamicClientRegistration` to `true` and add the `oidcClient()` plugin to the auth client configuration.

interview.answer: `onAPIError` is the Better Auth configuration object for API failures. Its documented options include throwing the error, invoking a custom handler, redirecting to an error URL, and customizing the default error page.
interview.followUp: How would you preserve the built-in error page while adding logging? Leave `errorURL` and page customization unchanged, and use `onError` only for the logging side effect.

interview.question: How do you configure API errors to throw?
interview.answer: Set `throw: true` to make an API error throw. The documented default is `false`, so throwing must be explicitly enabled.
interview.followUp: What happens if `throw` is omitted? Better Auth uses the documented default of `false`, so the configuration does not request thrown API errors.

interview.question: How can custom handling be added?
interview.answer: Use `onError` for custom error handling, such as logging the error and its context. The documented callback receives `(error, ctx)`.
interview.followUp: Which option controls the destination rather than callback behavior? `errorURL` specifies the URL used for redirecting on error.

interview.question: What does the oneTap plugin do?
interview.answer: oneTap is the server plugin that integrates Better Auth with Google's One Tap API. Configure it in betterAuth with the Google clientId, then pair it with oneTapClient on the client.
interview.followUp: What browser-side method starts the flow? Call authClient.oneTap(); the client plugin also supports a button configuration for rendering a Sign In with Google button.

interview.question: What configuration is required?
interview.answer: The current stable documentation requires a clientId for oneTap. The value should correspond to the Google OAuth web client configured for the application.
interview.followUp: Which Google Cloud setting is easy to overlook? Authorized JavaScript origins must include the application's origins, including localhost when developing.

interview.question: Which flow options are available?

interview.followUp: How can an application avoid the automatic prompt? Pass button options to authClient.oneTap() to render a Google sign-in button instead.

interview.question: What is a passkey?
interview.answer: Passkeys use WebAuthn-compatible cryptographic key pairs instead of passwords. The private key remains on the user's device, while the public key is associated with the website.
interview.followUp: Why are passkeys resistant to phishing? The credential is bound to the relying party, so a fraudulent site cannot use the legitimate site's credential.

interview.question: How do you enable passkeys in Better Auth?
interview.answer: Install @better-auth/passkey and add passkey() to the plugins array in betterAuth. Then migrate or generate the schema so the required passkey storage is available.
interview.followUp: What must be done before registration? The user must already be authenticated.

interview.question: Which client operations does the plugin expose?
interview.answer: Use authClient.signIn.passkey() to start passkey authentication. The same client API provides passkey.addPasskey for registration and listUserPasskeys for retrieving the authenticated user's passkeys.
interview.followUp: How can passkey sign-in be prepared when a component loads? Call authClient.signIn.passkey with autoFill set to true.

interview.question: What is the purpose of the Better Auth `secret` option?
interview.answer: The `secret` option is the key Better Auth uses for encryption, signing, and hashing. It can be supplied directly or through `BETTER_AUTH_SECRET` or `AUTH_SECRET`.
interview.followUp: What happens if no value is configured in production? Better Auth throws an error rather than continuing with the default.

interview.question: Which environment variables does Better Auth check?
interview.answer: Better Auth first looks for `process.env.BETTER_AUTH_SECRET`, then `process.env.AUTH_SECRET`. If neither exists, it uses its documented fallback value, although production should configure a real secret.
interview.followUp: How should a secret be generated? Use a high-entropy value; the documentation provides `openssl rand -base64 32`.

interview.question: How does `secret` relate to secret rotation?
interview.answer: The plural `secrets` option supports versioned secret rotation. During migration, the singular `secret` can remain as a fallback for decrypting legacy data within the same encryption purpose.
interview.followUp: Does retaining the old singular secret preserve every old state artifact? No; the documentation specifically excludes pending OAuth or SAML state cookies and OAuth Proxy payloads when changing to purpose-specific keys.

interview.question: How does Better Auth validate a normal session?
interview.answer: Better Auth stores the session in a cookie and sends it to the server on each request. The server verifies the session and returns user data only when the session is valid.
interview.followUp: How can session lookups avoid the primary database? Configure a secondary storage such as Redis; Better Auth checks it before falling back to the database.

interview.question: How do expiration and renewal differ?
interview.answer: The session expires after seven days by default. The expiresIn setting controls the lifetime, while updateAge determines when using the session causes its expiration to be extended.
interview.followUp: What happens when secondary storage is configured? Sessions are stored there instead of the database by default, unless storeSessionInDatabase is enabled.

interview.question: Which APIs manage an authenticated session?
interview.answer: getSession retrieves the active session, useSession provides reactive access, and revokeSession ends a session using its token. updateSession can change configured additional session fields.
interview.followUp: How would you support multiple active devices? Use listSessions to obtain the user's active sessions and revoke individual sessions by token.

Revoking a session requires supplying its session token.

interview.question: How do you update a user's profile information?
interview.answer: Call authClient.updateUser with an object containing the user fields that should change. The documented example passes image and name.
interview.followUp: How would you update only one field? Pass an object containing only that field, such as { name: "New Name" }, assuming the client supports the field.

interview.question: What object is used to invoke updateUser?
interview.answer: The method is exposed by the Better Auth client, so the client must already be configured and imported before calling it. The page demonstrates importing authClient from a local auth-client module.
interview.followUp: Where should client configuration live? In the application's shared Better Auth client module, which can then be imported wherever profile updates are needed.

interview.question: Which fields does the official example update?
interview.answer: The documented update payload includes image and name properties. The image value is a URL string, while name is the user's display-name string.
interview.followUp: What should be validated before sending an image URL? Validate the URL and any application-specific profile rules before invoking the client method.

keyPoints: Use the client-provided updateUser function to change the current user's information.
Pass the updates as a single object rather than as positional arguments.
The call is asynchronous, so await the returned operation when updating profile data.

User.summary: Better Auth’s User type is the inferred shape of an authenticated user object. Plugins and configured additional fields can extend it, with the resulting type available across server and client code.
User.explanation: Better Auth’s User type represents the authenticated user object returned with a session. Its shape can be extended by plugins and configured additional user fields, while the TypeScript inference system makes the resulting type available through the inferred API types.
User.syntax: type User = /* inferred Better Auth user object */
User.returns: The inferred authenticated user object shape, including fields contributed by plugins and configured additional fields.

interview.question: What does Better Auth’s User type represent?
interview.answer: The User type describes the user object associated with an authenticated session. Better Auth can extend it with plugin fields and configured additional fields, and those changes are reflected by type inference.
interview.followUp: How would you obtain the resulting shape? Use the relevant `$Infer` type exposed by the server or client, rather than recreating the base User type manually.

interview.question: Where does the User object appear in a session?
interview.answer: A session contains both a `session` object and a `user` object. The `user` property is the User-shaped value for the authenticated account.
interview.followUp: Why is this useful? Code handling authentication can access identity data and session metadata through their distinct inferred properties.

interview.question: How can the User type be extended safely?
interview.answer: Plugins and additional user fields can extend the base User type. Better Auth’s TypeScript inference makes those additions available on both the server and client.
interview.followUp: What should be checked when a custom field is missing from types? Verify that it was declared using the documented additional-fields configuration and that the generated inference is being used.

keyPoints: A session separates identity data under `user` from session metadata under `session`.
Installed plugins may add properties to the User type.
Use `$Infer` to obtain the User shape generated by the configured authentication system.
Configuration supports custom fields on both user and session records.
Declared custom fields remain type-safe across server and client code.
gotchas: Plugin-provided fields can change the effective User shape, so prefer Better Auth’s inference utilities instead of manually duplicating the type.
Additional user fields must be declared through the supported configuration so both server and client types include them.

username.summary: The username plugin adds username-based authentication to Better Auth’s email/password flow. It supports username signup, login, updates, availability checks, validation, length limits, and normalization.
username.explanation: The username plugin extends email/password authentication with username-based sign-in. Add it to the server, generate or run the database migration, and add the client plugin to use username signup, sign-in, updates, and availability checks.

example.title: Configure the username plugin
example.explanation: Enable email/password authentication and add the username plugin to the server configuration.

useCases.scenario: Allow users to register and authenticate without exposing email addresses as their login identifier.

useCases.scenario: Prevent duplicate names before completing registration or profile changes.

useCases.title: Username policy enforcement
useCases.scenario: Enforce product-specific naming rules with length and custom validation settings.

interview.question: What does the username plugin provide?
interview.answer: The username plugin adds username support to the email/password authenticator. It lets users sign in with a username rather than an email address.
interview.followUp: How would you make usernames unchangeable? Set immutableUsername to true in the plugin configuration.

interview.question: How is the plugin installed?
interview.answer: Configure username() in the server plugins array and include usernameClient() in the client plugins array. The database must also be migrated or generated with the plugin's required fields and tables.
interview.followUp: What must happen after adding the server plugin? Run the migration or generate the schema before using the feature.

interview.question: Which client operations does the plugin add?
interview.answer: The client exposes signUp.email with a username property for registration and signIn.username for username login. It also provides updateUser for changes and isUsernameAvailable for availability checks.
interview.followUp: What controls accepted names? Configure the minimum and maximum lengths and provide a validation function when the defaults are insufficient.

keyPoints: It extends the built-in email/password flow rather than replacing that authenticator.
Registration continues through signUp.email, with username included in the submitted data.
Username login uses the dedicated signIn.username client method.
Authenticated users can change their username through updateUser when mutability is allowed.
Availability can be checked before registration or a username change.
The default minimum username length is three characters.
The default maximum username length is thirty characters.
gotchas: After enabling the plugin, update the database schema before using username features.
Case differences do not create distinct usernames because values are lowercased by default.
Changing usernames remains possible unless immutableUsername is enabled.

verifyEmail.summary: `verifyEmail` completes manual email verification from a token in a custom verification link. Calling it with the token lets Better Auth verify the user's email.
verifyEmail.explanation: The client verifies an email by calling `verifyEmail` with a query object containing the token from the verification URL. After the user follows the link, Better Auth marks the email as verified and can redirect to the configured callback URL; custom post-verification work can run through `afterEmailVerification`.

parameters.description: Verification token passed in the query object; the token comes from the verification URL.

verifyEmail.returns: The documentation does not specify the method's response shape.

useCases.title: Link-based verification
useCases.scenario: An application uses the built-in verification URL so clicking the link verifies the address and redirects the user.

useCases.title: Post-verification workflow
useCases.scenario: An application needs to perform provisioning or notifications after verification completes.

interview.question: What does `authClient.verifyEmail` do?
interview.answer: `verifyEmail` completes manual email verification. The client receives the token in the query object, and Better Auth uses that token to verify the email.
interview.followUp: How can verification happen without calling this method directly? The user can open the generated verification URL, which verifies the email automatically and redirects to the configured callback URL.

interview.question: What input does the method require?
interview.answer: Call `authClient.verifyEmail({ query: { token } })`, where `token` is the verification token contained in the custom verification link.
interview.followUp: What should happen after verification? Configure `afterEmailVerification` to run custom code immediately after the email is verified.

interview.question: How does required verification affect sign-in?
interview.answer: When `require email verification` is enabled, users must verify their email before logging in. Verification is initiated through the configured email-sending flow, and the verification token completes it.
interview.followUp: When is the sender invoked during sign-in? The documentation says `sendVerificationEmail` is called every time a user tries to sign in when verification is required.

keyPoints: Following the supplied verification URL can complete verification automatically and redirect the user to `callbackURL`.
Use `afterEmailVerification` for application-specific work that must run immediately after successful verification.
The email sender receives a data object containing the user, including the address that needs verification.
gotchas: Manual verification requires putting the token into a custom link and then passing it to `verifyEmail`.
Enabling required verification blocks users from signing in until their email is verified.

interview.question: How do you configure Zoom sign-in?
interview.answer: Add a zoom entry inside socialProviders with clientId and clientSecret values, then call the client’s signIn.social method using provider: "zoom". The provider credentials come from the Zoom app configuration.
interview.followUp: What OAuth app setting is needed beyond credentials? The Zoom app must include the Better Auth callback URL under OAuth Redirect URL.

interview.question: How does the client start Zoom authentication?
interview.answer: The client sign-in call is await authClient.signIn.social({ provider: "zoom" }). This selects Zoom as the OAuth provider for the authentication flow.
interview.followUp: Which permission should the Zoom app include? The documented setup instructs selecting the user:read:user scope and adding other application-required scopes.

interview.question: What preparation is required in Zoom before configuring Better Auth?
interview.answer: Create a Zoom Marketplace General App, choose User-managed, copy its Client ID and Client Secret, and configure the OAuth redirect URL. Then pass those credentials to Better Auth’s zoom provider configuration.
interview.followUp: Where should credentials be stored? The page instructs copying them and storing them in a safe location; the example reads them from environment variables.

keyPoints: The page is dedicated to setting up and using Zoom as a Better Auth social provider.
Zoom is configured by adding its provider object to the auth instance’s socialProviders option.
The provider configuration supplies the Zoom client ID from an environment variable.
The provider configuration supplies the Zoom client secret from an environment variable.

gotchas: The callback URL configured in the Zoom app must match the application's callback endpoint.
